I’ve been farming this 7.5 mu plot in Quzhou for 35 years, so I know every ridge and how the well water holds up in a dry July. With only three mouths to feed and no hired hands, I have to keep the workload tight but the income steady. My bread‑and‑butter is the cabbage‑chili relay on 3 mu: I’ll put spring cabbage in the ground now, get it off by early June, and then transplant chili seedlings straight onto the same beds. That double‑crop squeeze is what pays the bills. The remaining 4.5 mu I split between eggplant, kidney bean and maize—eggplant brings good cash at the village market, kidney bean is light work and fixes a bit of nitrogen, and maize is my safety grain if vegetable prices crash. I always buy hybrid seed for cabbage, chili, eggplant and maize from the county co‑op; the yield jump is worth the extra yuan, and I can’t afford a bad year. For beans I use an improved local variety. I rotary‑till everything—fast, easy with my small tiller, and the seedbed comes out fine. I’ll lay down compound fertilizer as a base and top‑dress nitrogen when the plants start running. Because I have the well, I water whenever the top soil dries; vegetables can’t wait for rain. I spray preventively too—one bad aphid or borer outbreak on the cabbage or chili and the whole season’s profit rots in the field.
